title: Wire Size for 1.5 Ton AC (mm² & 7/29) + Breaker | Wattlyst
meta: Which wire and breaker for a 1.5 ton inverter or non-inverter AC? mm² and 3/29, 7/29 sizes, run length and safety margin, explained.
author: ali-ahmad

sections.h2: What breaker size for a 1.5 ton AC?
p: A 16 A type C MCB for both the inverter and the non-inverter 1.5 ton. The inverter's design current is 9.2 A at its 1,900 W maximum input; a compressor runs near full current for hours, so the breaker is chosen at 9.2 A × 1.25 = 11.5 A, which rounds up to 16 A. A smaller MCB would run close to its limit on a hot day and trip for no fault.

The non-inverter 1.5 ton draws 9.8 A while running and several times that for a moment at every compressor start. A type C curve tolerates that surge; a type B of the same rating may trip on the start. For a 1 ton inverter the MCB drops to 10 A.

sections.h2: What wire size for a 1 ton AC?
p: 2.5 mm² copper (7/29), the minimum for any AC circuit, with a 10 A type C MCB. A 1 ton inverter has a maximum input of 1,200 W and a design current of 5.8 A, so a 10 m run drops only 0.5%. Do not go down to 3/29 to save money: it is a lighting size and below the minimum for an AC.

sections.h2: What wire size for a 2 ton AC?
p: Still 2.5 mm² (7/29) for most homes, with a 16 A type C MCB. A 2 ton inverter has a maximum input of 2,500 W, a design current of 12.1 A, and even over a 30 m run the voltage drop is 2.8%, within the 5% limit. The 2 ton non-inverter is different: its 20 A MCB is above what 7/29 carries in 45 °C air, so it needs 4 mm² (7/36). On very long runs, or where several cables share a conduit, enter that above and the calculator moves up a size.

sections.h2: Is 7/29 wire enough for an AC?
p: Yes for 1 ton and 1.5 ton ACs and a 2 ton inverter on a normal run. 7/29 is seven copper strands and is rated here as a 2.5 mm² cable, able to carry 19 A in conduit in 45 °C air, above the 16 A a 1.5 ton inverter circuit needs. A 2 ton non-inverter needs 4 mm² (7/36) in that heat. It is also the minimum size allowed for an AC circuit, so nothing smaller is acceptable whatever the AC.

7/29 stops being enough when the run is long enough for the voltage drop to pass 5%, or when the cable is derated for grouping or heat. Enter your own run length above; the calculator moves to 7/36 when it has to.

sections.h2: Does summer heat change the AC wire size?
p: Yes. Cable ratings in the IEC table are for 30 °C air. In 45 °C air a PVC cable keeps only 0.79 of that rating, so 7/29 drops from 24 A to 19 A. That still covers a 1.5 ton AC on a 16 A MCB, but not a 2 ton non-inverter on a 20 A MCB, which needs 4 mm² (7/36).

The default air temperature is a cautious summer value for cable in a roof or outside wall; it is waiting for review by a PEC-registered engineer. Set your own above, and if other circuits share the conduit, enter how many in Advanced settings.

sections.h2: Which wire should I use for an AC: 3/29, 7/29 or 7/36?
p: Use copper only, never aluminium or copper-clad wire for an AC. 3/29 is a lighting size and is never used for an AC circuit. 7/29 (2.5 mm²) is the standard AC wire for 1 ton and 1.5 ton units and 2 ton inverters on ordinary runs. 7/36 is the next size up for long runs, hot roof spaces or cables grouped in one conduit, and costs little more.

Whatever the size, run it as a dedicated circuit from the distribution board with its own MCB and an earth wire of the same size, and fit a socket or isolator rated for the current. Buy cable from a known maker with the size printed on the sheath.

sections.h2: Why does the run length change the AC wiring size in mm²?
p: Every metre of cable has resistance, so some voltage is lost on the way to the AC and back. At 15 m a 1.5 ton inverter loses 2.5 V (1.1%); at 30 m the 2 ton inverter loses 2.8%. The limit for a power circuit is 5%: above it the compressor runs hot, starts badly and wastes energy, so the calculator picks the next cable size that brings the drop back under the limit.
Measure the run along the walls and ceiling, not across the room, and include the drop from the ceiling to the indoor unit and the run to the outdoor unit if it is fed from the same cable.

faq.q: Which wire is best for a 1.5 ton inverter AC?
faq.a: 2.5 mm² copper, sold as 7/29 in Pakistan, on a dedicated circuit with a 16 A type C MCB. It carries 19 A in conduit in 45 °C air against the 16 A the circuit needs.

faq.q: Can I use 7/29 wire for a 2 ton AC?
faq.a: For a 2 ton inverter, yes: it needs 2.5 mm² (7/29) with a 16 A type C MCB even over 30 m, with a 2.8% drop. A 2 ton non-inverter gets a 20 A MCB, and in 45 °C air 7/29 is rated only 19 A, so it needs 4 mm² (7/36).

faq.q: What breaker for an inverter AC?
faq.a: A type C MCB at the next standard size above the design current times 1.25: 16 A for a 1.5 ton inverter, 10 A for a 1 ton inverter and 16 A for a 2 ton inverter.

faq.q: Does an inverter AC need a thinner wire than a non-inverter?
faq.a: No. Both 1.5 ton types get 2.5 mm² and a 16 A type C MCB. The inverter's maximum input of 1,900 W is actually a little above the non-inverter's 1,800 W running load; the non-inverter's extra is a short start surge the C curve handles.

faq.q: Is a lighting wire (3/29) enough for a small AC?
faq.a: No. The minimum for any AC circuit is 2.5 mm², which is 7/29. 3/29 is rated as 1 mm² and is for lighting points only.

faq.q: How far can the AC be from the distribution board on 7/29?
faq.a: Far enough for most homes: the 2 ton inverter example at 30 m drops 2.8% against a 5% limit. Enter your own run length and the calculator moves to the next size when the drop goes over the limit.

faq.q: Do I need a separate breaker for each AC?
faq.a: Yes. Each AC gets its own cable from the distribution board and its own type C MCB, so a fault on one AC does not cut the others and the cable is protected by a breaker sized for it.

key_facts: For a 1.5 ton inverter AC on a 15 m run the cable is 2.5 mm² copper (7/29) and the breaker is a 16 A type C MCB on a dedicated circuit.
An inverter AC is sized at its maximum input (1,900 W for a 1.5 ton), not its average draw, because on a hot afternoon it runs at full speed for long periods.
A 1.5 ton non-inverter AC runs at about 1,800 W but its compressor start surge is several times that, so it gets a C-curve MCB of 16 A on the same 2.5 mm² cable.
The minimum cable for any AC circuit is 2.5 mm² (7/29); longer runs need a thicker cable to keep the voltage drop under 5%.
mistakes: Sizing an inverter AC at its average draw. The average is for the bill; the cable and MCB must carry the maximum input of 1,900 W for hours on a hot day.
Using 3/29 or aluminium wire. 3/29 is a lighting size below the 2.5 mm² minimum for an AC circuit, and aluminium needs a larger size and special terminals.
Sharing the circuit. An AC on a socket circuit with other loads overloads the cable and trips the MCB; every AC gets its own cable and MCB from the distribution board.
Measuring the run in a straight line. Cable follows the walls and ceiling, so the real run, and the voltage drop, is often half as long again.

Ignoring heat and grouping. A cable in a hot roof conduit, or several circuits in one conduit, carries less current than the table value; enter the air temperature and the number of circuits above and the calculator derates the cable.

The cable must be rated at least 16 A and be at least 2.5 mm² for an AC circuit: 2.5 mm² (7/29) is rated 19 A for this installation: 24 A in the IEC table at 30 °C × 0.79 for 45 °C air and 1 circuit in the conduit. examples.title: Split AC 1.5 ton inverter, 15 m in conduit
examples.text: Maximum input 1,900 W ÷ (230 V × 0.9) = 9.2 A; × 1.25 = 11.5 A, so a 16 A type C MCB. Cable: 2.5 mm² (7/29), rated 19 A. Voltage drop 1.1%.

examples.title: Split AC 1.5 ton non-inverter, 15 m in conduit
examples.text: Running 1,800 W ÷ (230 V × 0.8) = 9.8 A; × 1.25 = 12.2 A, so a 16 A type C MCB that rides through the compressor start. Cable: 2.5 mm² (7/29), rated 19 A. Voltage drop 1.1%.

examples.title: Split AC 2 ton inverter on a long 30 m run
examples.text: Maximum input 2,500 W gives 12.1 A and a 16 A type C MCB. 2.5 mm² (7/29) still works: the drop over 30 m is 6.5 V, or 2.8%, under the 5% limit.

examples.title: Split AC 1 ton inverter, 10 m in conduit
examples.text: Maximum input 1,200 W gives 5.8 A; × 1.25 = 7.2 A, so a 10 A type C MCB. The cable stays at the AC minimum of 2.5 mm² (7/29); voltage drop 0.5%.

examples.title: Split AC 2 ton non-inverter, 15 m in conduit, 45 °C air
examples.text: Running 2,400 W ÷ (230 V × 0.8) = 13 A; × 1.25 = 16.3 A, so a 20 A type C MCB. In 45 °C air every cable keeps 0.79 of its table rating, so the cable is 4 mm² (7/36), rated 25 A (32 A in the table). Voltage drop 1%.

content.answer: A 1.5 ton inverter AC needs a 2.5 mm² copper cable (7/29 in Pakistani sizes) on its own 16 A MCB (type C for compressors) for a 15 m run in conduit. It is sized at the AC's maximum input of 1,900 W: 9.2 A design current with a 1.25 × margin, and the voltage drop is only 1.1%.

formula.text: I_b = P ÷ (V × PF); I_n ≥ I_b × margin; I_z ≥ max(I_b × margin, I_n); ΔV% = 2 × L × I_b × ρ ÷ A ÷ V × 100
lines: I_b = design current; P = the AC's maximum input (inverter) or running watts (non-inverter)
I_n = MCB rating, the next standard size; I_z = cable current rating for the installation method
L = one-way cable run in metres; ρ = resistivity of copper; A = cable area in mm²
ΔV% must stay under the limit for power circuits; minimum 2.5 mm² for an AC circuit

content.safety: These sizes are planning values for copper cable in 45 °C air with 1 circuit in the conduit; the air temperature default is a cautious summer value still awaiting review by a PEC-registered engineer. A licensed electrician must confirm the cable, the earth and the MCB on site, check the real heat and grouping, and connect the AC to a dedicated circuit.
